amendments.rule: An intensive `αὐτός` that the ASV renders by a **two-word English emphatic** is one `aligned` unit headed on the ***-self*** word, never on the plain pronoun standing in front of it. `αὐτοὶ` → *they themselves* heads on *themselves*, as `αὐτὸς` → *he himself* heads on *himself* in ten corpus units, `αὐτὸς` → *I myself* on *myself* at PHP.2.24, `αὐτὸς` → *his own self* on *self* at 1PE.2.24, and `αὐτοῦ` → *own self* on *self* at ROM.16.2; discontinuity changes nothing, HEB.2.14's *he … himself* being one unit under rule 15. Rule 17 is what decides it: the *-self* word is what realizes the intensive force the pronoun carries, while the *he*, *she*, *they* or *I* beside it is the subject word English syntax requires and rides inside the unit as a rule 7 or rule 9 helper. So this is not the genuine tie rule 17 lets English word order break, and a head on the plain pronoun is not a materially different analysis under rule 16. The corpus is thirteen units to four, and of the four JHN.6.6 and MRK.10.12 concede this reading in their own notes, ROM.16.2 heads its own second `αὐτός` on *self* in the same verse, and only REV.19.12 argues the point, on a tie this rule denies. Where the ASV writes a **single** English word the question does not arise and that word is the head, as the units of *himself*, *itself*, *myself*, *thyself* and *herself* are, and as `αὐτὸς` → *selfsame* is. A **personal pronoun** — `ἐγώ`, `σύ`, `ἡμεῖς`, `ὑμεῖς` — that the ASV expands with a supplied *-self* word is the contrast and goes the other way, headed on the **pronoun**: `Ὑμεῖς` → *Ye yourselves* heads on *Ye* in all five of its corpus units, as `ἡμεῖς` → *we ourselves* heads on *we* at 2PE.1.18 and TIT.3.5 and `ἐγὼ` → *I myself* on *I* at PHP.3.4 and 2CO.12.16 — nine units against none. The test is the one this rule already applies, which of the two words answers to the source lexeme: `αὐτός` **is** the intensive, so the *-self* word realizes it and the plain pronoun beside it is what English syntax requires, whereas a personal pronoun is what *ye*, *we* or *I* spells and the *-self* word beside it is the supplied intensifier, a rule 7 helper riding inside the unit. So the lexeme and not the English phrase decides, which is why the identical *Ye yourselves* heads on *Ye* for `Ὑμεῖς` at ACT.20.18 and on *yourselves* for `αὐτοὶ` at ACT.20.34, one chapter writing both. Where the ASV instead writes a **separate** word for each token the pair splits like any other and each keeps its own head, `ὑμῶν αὐτῶν` → *your own selves* giving *your* to `ὑμῶν` and *own selves* to `αὐτῶν` headed on *selves*; and where **one** English word stands for both tokens the question does not arise, `ὑμῖν αὐτοῖς` → *yourselves* being one `aligned` unit on that word. An `αὐτός` carrying no intensive force is untouched by this rule: an oblique pronoun is aligned in the ordinary way, and a genitive one carries the English possessive and displaces its article under rule 20.
amendments.why: Rule 107 is scoped in terms to intensive αὐτός and says nothing about a personal pronoun the ASV expands the same way, so a verse pass meeting Ὑμεῖς → 'Ye yourselves' has only rule 17 to go on and can read rule 107's 'never on the plain pronoun' across to it. ACT.20 writes both phrasings with the identical English — 20:18 from Ὑμεῖς, 20:34 from αὐτοί — which is what made the gap visible. The corpus decides it without dissent: ye yourselves heads on ye in 5 units, we ourselves on we in 2, I myself on I in 2, none the other way, against rule 107's own 13 for αὐτός. The added clause states the test rule 107 already uses rather than a second test, and closes with the two configurations (separate words, single word) that ACT.20.30 and the ὑμῖν αὐτοῖς units would otherwise leave open.

amendments.rule: A **pleonastic negative** in the complement clause of a verb of denial is its own `unrepresented` unit. `ὁ ἀρνούμενος ὅτι Ἰησοῦς οὐκ ἔστιν ὁ χριστός` → *he that denieth that Jesus is the Christ* leaves `οὐκ` empty, because Greek doubles the denial into the complement and English does not, so no part of any English word answers to the particle and rule 23 decides it on its own terms. Rules 41 and 59 are the shape but not the licence, and the difference is the whole of this rule: what licenses those is a second **negative word** able to carry the English negation alone, and here there is none — what absorbs the particle is the lexeme of `ἀρνέομαι` itself. So do not cite them, and do not manufacture a word for the particle by stretching it onto *denieth*, which answers wholly to the participle; the corpus renders `ἀρνέομαι` *deny*, *denied*, *denieth* and *denying* throughout and never with a negative component of its own. The same holds for the redundant `μή` Greek writes in the **infinitival complement of a verb of withholding, hindering or refusing**, which English likewise does not double: `οὐδὲν ὑπεστειλάμην … τοῦ μὴ ἀναγγεῖλαι ὑμῖν` → *I shrank not from declaring unto you anything* and `οὐ … ὑπεστειλάμην τοῦ μὴ ἀναγγεῖλαι ὑμῖν` → *I shrank not from declaring unto you* both leave `μή` empty, the verb's own lexeme absorbing it exactly as `ἀρνέομαι` absorbs the other, and the nominalizing article of the infinitive standing `unrepresented` beside it under rule 61. The clause's one English negation then belongs to whichever token carries it in the ordinary way — `οὐ` → *not*, or the discontinuous *not … anything* to `οὐδέν` under rules 15 and 69 where no plain negator stands. Do not move that *not* onto the `μή` merely because the particle stands next to the infinitive it negates. A negative the ASV does realize is untouched by this rule and is aligned in the ordinary way, as `καὶ οὐκ ἠρνήσατο` → *and he denied not* is. A reference comparison will report the `unrepresented` particle as a disagreement, and that report is not a correction.
amendments.why: Rule 79's text is scoped to a verb of denial and grounds itself on ἀρνέομαι's lexeme, so a verse meeting τοῦ μὴ ἀναγγεῖλαι after ὑποστέλλομαι has to reason by analogy or fall back on bare rule 23 — and the temptation the rule was written to block, moving the clause's 'not' onto the redundant particle, is exactly what the reference alignment does at both ACT.20.20 and ACT.20.27. The widened class is the same Greek construction with the same English consequence: a verb of withholding or hindering doubles its negation into the complement and English writes it once. ACT.20 supplies two units, one with a plain οὐ carrying the negation and one with οὐδέν carrying it, so the amendment can say where the 'not' does go as well as where it does not. Nothing in the corpus shown contradicts it, and the rule keeps its own safeguard that a negative the ASV realizes is untouched.

conventions: The supplied English 'and' that the ASV must write once it has converted a Greek circumstantial participle into a finite clause is a rule 88 helper on the finite verb it introduces, and never `added`, even where that verb stands several tokens away behind a subordinate clause the ASV placed in front of it. ACT.20 carries nine such junctures — 20:1 ἐξῆλθεν, 20:3 γενομένης, 20:5 ἔμενον, 20:9 ἔπεσεν, 20:10 ἐπέπεσεν, 20:14 ἤλθομεν, 20:17 μετεκαλέσατο, 20:36 προσηύξατο, 20:37 κατεφίλουν — and not one is `added`. Rule 98 is the contrast and its test is the constituents joined, not the word standing immediately in front of the juncture: at 20:9 a participial phrase stands there and the seam is still clause-level, joining the converted 'there sat' to the expressed ἔπεσεν.

Rule 73 leaves the source head of a collapsed light-verb pair open, and ACT.20 puts it on the noun in all three of its pairs: ἐγένετο γνώμης → 'determined' at 20:3, θεὶς τὰ γόνατα → 'kneeled down' at 20:36, and ἐγένετο κλαυθμός → 'wept' at 20:37. In each the single English verb realizes the noun's lexeme and not the general verb's, which is the test rule 73 states. The article and the genitive pronoun inside 20:36's phrase stay their own `unrepresented` units under rules 23 and 93, the collapsed unit absorbing neither.

report: Checked all 62 candidate groups. Almost every difference is licensed by the ASV's own wording or by the source: τε aligned where no καί answers it (20:3, 20:7, 20:11, 20:35) and split with καί where the ASV writes 'both … and' (20:21); ἐπί aligned to 'yet' at 20:9 where the ASV writes two words and unrepresented at 20:11 where it writes none (rules 36, 94); preverb particles kept inside the verb at 20:6 and 20:29 because the expressed ἀπό and εἰς already carry complete English of their own (rule 106's addition arm); the substantival-article-before-participle family analysed one way throughout (20:20 empty because οὐδέν wrote the pronoun, 20:22 'the things', 20:32 'them', 20:34 'to them', 20:35 'the'); the three collapsed light-verb pairs all headed on the noun (20:3, 20:36, 20:37); οὐδείς rendered 'not … any(thing)' as one discontinuous unit at both 20:20 and 20:24.

One genuine split, invisible to the lemma table because it turns on an added unit. The supplied clause-coordinating 'and' is folded onto the finite verb it introduces in eight verses (20:1 ἐξῆλθεν, 20:3 γενομένης, 20:5 ἔμενον, 20:10 ἐπέπεσεν, 20:14 ἤλθομεν, 20:17 μετεκαλέσατο, 20:36 προσηύξατο, 20:37 κατεφίλουν) and marked added at 20:9. Rule 98's test does not fit 20:9: the seam joins the clause realizing καθεζόμενος, which the ASV converted into the finite 'there sat', to the expressed finite ἔπεσεν — not two like constituents both rendered alike — and the ASV's semicolon shows the coordination is clause-level. That is rule 88's shape. Patched: t018 now rides inside ἔπεσεν's unit under rule 15, and ACT.20.9 carries no added unit.

BSB: all 17 disagreements are documented convention differences and none is a genuine error. Fifteen are unrepresented articles or pronouns under rules 20, 21, 23, 31, 32, 38, 47, 57 and 93 — displaced determiners (20:28 τοῦ before ἰδίου, 20:32 τῆς, 20:34 ταῖς, 20:37 τόν), second attributive articles (20:19, 20:23, 20:28, 20:32), determinerless phrases (20:6 τῶν ἀζύμων, 20:32 τῷ θεῷ), an article before a name (20:37), and the article and αὐτοῦ absorbed by the collapsed idiom at 20:36. The remaining two are the pleonastic μή at 20:20 and 20:27 and ἐφ' ἱκανόν at 20:11, both of which the contract decides against the reference. No accepted edge was changed to improve the rate.

Not a split, though it looks like one: 20:18 Ὑμεῖς → 'Ye yourselves' heads on 'Ye' while 20:34 αὐτοί → 'Ye yourselves' heads on 'yourselves'. Rule 107 is scoped in terms to intensive αὐτός, and the corpus heads a personal pronoun expanded with a supplied -self word on the pronoun in all nine of its units (ye yourselves 5, we ourselves 2, I myself 2) with none the other way. The chapter writing both is what makes the distinction worth stating, so it is returned as an amendment to rule 107 rather than a convention.

Also checked and found licensed: the two supplied 'with' repetitions at 20:19 (rule 103), the supplied 'the son' folded onto Πύρρου at 20:4 (rule 52), the two supplied 'you' folded onto the infinitives at 20:32 (rule 7), and 20:3's 'there*', which no token of the verse licenses and is correctly added under rule 5.
